blocks.title: Hydrocarbons
blocks.text: Hydrocarbons are compounds that contain carbon and hydrogen only.

items: Open-chain (acyclic) hydrocarbons are usually called aliphatic hydrocarbons (from the Greek aleiphatos, fat, because fats have open-chain structures). They are saturated (alkanes) or unsaturated (alkenes and alkynes).

blocks.alt: A small yellow box: an oval labelled 'Aliphatic', a plus sign and an oval labelled 'Cyclic', joined by lines to a rectangle below labelled 'Alicyclic'.
blocks.caption: Aliphatic + cyclic: alicyclic (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

items: Closed-chain (cyclic) hydrocarbons contain rings of carbon atoms. Alicyclic hydrocarbons, saturated or unsaturated, behave like aliphatic ones, e.g. cycloalkanes and cycloalkenes. Aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring or a similar structure, e.g. benzene, naphthalene and diphenylmethane.

blocks.alt: Two groups separated by a thick line. Aliphatic hydrocarbons: CH3-CH3 (ethane), H2C=CH2 (ethene), HC triple-bond CH (ethyne) and a hexagon (cyclohexane). Aromatic hydrocarbons, each ring drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside: benzene, methyl benzene (CH3 on the ring), naphthalene (two fused rings) and anthracene (three fused rings in a row).
blocks.caption: Examples of aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: Classify methylcyclohexane, a methylcyclohexene, methylbenzene, naphthalene and cyclohexane as aliphatic, alicyclic or aromatic.
